transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. I suppose what brings me in is... well, I keep hearing these very clear voices. It happens mostly in my apartment, but also sometimes when I'm at the museum, you know, in those empty rooms where they keep the older exhibits. It sounds like women whispering, coming right from behind the walls. They tell me exactly which photographs belong in the archive. 

Speaking of archives, I actually used to spend hours organizing my old college photos. I got my bachelor's degree back in the eighties, and we used actual film back then. The smell of the developing fluid, it was just... it gets right into your clothes. I had this one sweater, a lovely blue cardigan, that smelled like chemicals for years. I think I finally gave it to Goodwill when they opened that new donation center down the street from the bakery. They make the most wonderful almond croissants there, by the way. Have you ever tried them? They flake perfectly if you get them before nine in the morning. But yes, the whispering women behind the walls... they just won't stop talking about the photographs.
How long have you been hearing these whispering voices?

Oh, it's been about... well, eight months now, I'd say. Eight months of the voices, and also this absolute certainty I have that people are watching my archive. I know it was eight months ago because it started right around the time I was picking out a new wall calendar for the kitchen. 

I always buy the ones with the little painted cottages, you know, the ones with the glowing yellow windows? They just look so cozy when you're making your morning tea. I tried a floral calendar a few years back, but the peonies for the month of May just looked a bit too loud, if that makes sense. It threw off the whole energy of my breakfasts. I actually had to take a pair of scissors and cut May right out of the binding. But yes, it's been about eight months of them whispering and watching the photographs.
During these past eight months, have you experienced any significant periods where your mood felt extremely low or, conversely, unusually elevated or energetic?

Oh, absolutely. There are these stretches of days where I just feel... radiant. Completely radiant and chosen, like I have this grand, brilliant purpose. It’s a bit like how the light catches that heavy crystal bowl I keep on my dining table. 

I found it at an estate sale over in Westbridge—oh, you should have seen the house, Dr. Smith. Mid-century modern, gorgeous teak wood everywhere, and the woman who owned it had this massive collection of vintage salt cellars. I almost bought a little silver one shaped like a swan, but I thought, really, who uses salt cellars anymore? It’s all those heavy grinders now. I bought one of those Himalayan pink salt grinders once, but the salt chunks were too big and it completely ruined a perfectly good batch of potato soup. Potatoes need a very fine salt, don't you think? Especially if you use the Yukon Golds. They have that buttery texture that just absorbs everything. 

But... oh, the moods, right. Yes, when I'm having one of those radiant days, I have so much energy for my plans. But if someone questions what I'm doing, or tells me I need to slow down, I become absolutely furious. Just enraged. It feels exactly as if they are trying to erase me.
During these past eight months, have there been any periods where the whispering voices continued even when you were not feeling that radiant, high-energy mood?

Well, yes, actually. I remember specifically there was a stretch... oh, it must have been several weeks where I didn't feel that radiant energy at all. I was just feeling quite normal, really, not grand or full of plans, but the whispering women were still there in the apartment. And I was still absolutely convinced that the arts people were monitoring my phone. 

I actually had to change my phone case because of it. I had this lovely floral one, with little hydrangeas painted on the back. Hydrangeas are so temperamental, aren't they? I tried growing them in my front planter box a few years ago, but the soil acidity was all wrong. You have to put coffee grounds in the soil if you want them to turn that beautiful deep blue. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she has the most stunning blue hydrangeas. But she uses some sort of chemical fertilizer, which I just refuse to do. It’s terrible for the bees. We have so few bees left as it is. I read an article in the Sunday paper about how the bumblebee population is just plummeting. I always save the Sunday paper for the crossword puzzle. I use a blue pen—never black, black feels too severe for a Sunday morning. 

But yes, the phone. Even when I wasn't feeling particularly energized, I knew they were listening through it, and the whispering in the walls just kept going on and on.
Aside from the times you felt radiant or energetic, have you experienced any periods where you felt deeply sad, hopeless, or lost interest in the things you usually enjoy?

Well, yes, I suppose there have been times like that, too. Not the radiant days, but... quiet days. Very quiet. There are these long stretches where I just sit at my kitchen table, staring out the window. My little herb pots on the windowsill just sit there drying out, and I don't even water them. 

I usually take such good care of my herbs. I have basil, thyme, and this wonderful lemon balm that smells just heavenly if you rub the leaves between your fingers. You can actually make a very soothing tea out of lemon balm, you know. My grandmother used to make it for me when I couldn't sleep. She had this beautiful old copper kettle that she'd boil the water in. It had a whistle that sounded almost like a train in the distance. I tried to find a copper kettle like that at an antique shop last year, but they all had these modern plastic handles that just ruined the look entirely. It's such a shame how things are made these days, everything is plastic. Even the little pots the herbs come in at the nursery are plastic now. I always transplant mine into terracotta. Terracotta breathes so much better, it prevents root rot. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Right, the quiet days. Yes, I just sit there while the herbs dry out. I don't call my friends back. Sometimes someone will invite me out—to a concert, or maybe a gallery opening, which I usually adore—but I just don't feel any interest at all. I just sit there at the table.
During those quiet, sad periods when you lost interest in your hobbies and the herbs dried out, did the whispering voices continue to occur?

Well... you know, I really can't say for sure. It's so hard to remember what's happening when I get like that, when the days just blur together. It's a bit like when you try to remember a dream right after you wake up, but the harder you grasp at it, the faster it slips away. 

I actually keep a dream journal on my nightstand to help with that. It has a beautiful embossed leather cover—I got it at a little artisan market downtown. The woman who made it hand-binds all her books using this traditional Italian technique. She had this fascinating story about how she lived in Florence for three years learning from a master bookbinder. Florence must be incredible. I've always wanted to visit Italy, especially Tuscany, to see the rolling hills and the vineyards. I hear the wine there is just spectacular. Though honestly, I've never been much of a wine drinker. A glass of Pinot Noir always gives me a terrible headache the next morning. My sister swears by taking a vitamin B complex before drinking wine to prevent the headaches, but she's always falling for those sorts of holistic remedies. She once tried to convince me to put raw onion in my socks to cure a cold! Can you imagine? 

But anyway... about the whispering on those quiet days... I just really haven't noticed one way or the other. When I'm sitting there at the table, everything is just sort of... blank.

Looking back over the last eight months, can you recall a period of at least two weeks where you felt neither 'radiant' nor 'sad,' but just like your usual self, yet the voices and the feeling of being watched were still present?

Well, yes, actually. I think I mentioned this just a little bit ago... there was that stretch, oh, it must have been several weeks, where I wasn't feeling radiant or grand at all. And I wasn't feeling sad and quiet either. I was just... me. Just going about my day. But the whispering women, they were still there in the apartment with me. And I was still absolutely certain the arts people were listening to my phone. 

Which is why I changed the case, remember? The floral one. I do miss that case sometimes, the hydrangeas were so pretty. I saw a woman at the grocery store yesterday with a sweater that had the exact same shade of blue hydrangeas embroidered on the collar. It was such a lovely piece, it looked vintage. I love finding vintage clothes. There used to be this marvelous little consignment shop on Elm Street—oh, they had the most exquisite silk scarves. I bought one there once that was supposedly owned by a famous jazz singer in the fifties. I used to tie it around my neck when I went for drives in the autumn. The autumn air here gets so crisp, doesn't it? You really need a good scarf. I always pack my summer clothes away on Labor Day weekend, it's just a tradition I have. 

But yes, to answer your question, there were definitely a few weeks where I felt perfectly normal, not high or low, but the whispering and the monitoring... that didn't stop.
During the times you felt that 'radiant' energy, did you also experience a decreased need for sleep, such as feeling fully rested after only a few hours of sleep for several days in a row?

Oh, absolutely. During those radiant days, sleep just seems so... unnecessary. I can lay down for maybe two or three hours, and I'll wake up before dawn feeling completely ready for the day. I just tell myself that sleep is for people who do not have an archive to rescue. 

And dawn is such a beautiful time of day anyway. The light is so soft and pearlescent before the sun really comes up. I used to paint a lot of sunrises when I was younger. I had this set of watercolors that my father brought back from a business trip to Germany. They were in this elegant little tin box with a thumb ring on the bottom so you could hold it while you painted outdoors. Plein air painting, they call it. The French have such lovely words for things. I tried to take a French class at the community center a few years ago, but the instructor was this dreadful man who kept insisting we roll our R's like we were in Spain. It was terribly confusing. I ended up dropping the class and taking up knitting instead. I knit a whole afghan that winter, mostly in shades of teal and mustard yellow. It's draped over the back of my sofa right now. 

But yes, when I'm feeling that radiant energy, two or three hours is really all I need, and then I'm up and moving.

During those radiant periods when you had so much energy and needed so little sleep, did your behavior ever become so intense or unmanageable that it caused serious problems at work, forced you to stop your usual activities, or resulted in you needing help from a hospital or clinic?

Well, yes, it did get quite out of hand. I suppose I did lose the trust of my colleagues... I missed several important board meetings and just completely forgot to pay my bills. It got to the point where my cousin and one of the museum administrators had to step in. They had to take over because I just couldn't manage my appointments, or my money, or even attend public events safely by myself. 

Speaking of public events, I used to love going to the symphony. The strings section always gave me goosebumps. My cousin actually plays the cello, quite beautifully too. She has this antique cello that's been in our family for generations, supposedly made in the 1800s. It has such a rich, resonant sound. We used to go to this little tea shop after her recitals. They served the most delicate cucumber sandwiches with the crusts cut off, just like they do in England. I've always admired British etiquette, it's so refined. Did you know they have specific rules for how to stir tea? You're supposed to move the spoon back and forth from six o'clock to twelve o'clock, never in a circle. It's fascinating how many little unspoken rules there are in society. 

But yes, when I had all that energy, I really couldn't manage things on my own, and it caused quite a few problems until they stepped in to help me.

And dawn is such a beautiful time of day anyway. The light is so soft and pearlescent before the sun really comes up. I used to paint a lot of sunrises when I was younger. I had this set of watercolors that my father brought back from a business trip to Germany. They were in this elegant little tin box with a thumb ring on the bottom so you could hold it while you painted outdoors. Plein air painting, they call it. The French have such lovely words for things. I tried to take a French class at the community center a few years ago, but the instructor was this dreadful man who kept insisting we roll our R's like we were in Spain. It was terribly confusing. I ended up dropping the class and taking up knitting instead. I knit a whole afghan that winter, mostly in shades of teal and mustard yellow. It's draped over the back of my sofa right now. 

But yes, when I'm feeling that radiant energy, two or three hours is really all I need, and then I'm up and moving.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has ever experienced a full Manic Episode (which would point to F25.2) versus a Hypomanic Episode (which would point to F25.0 or F25.1), specifically by asking about significant functional impairment or hospitalization during the high-energy periods.
doctor.question: During those radiant periods when you had so much energy and needed so little sleep, did your behavior ever become so intense or unmanageable that it caused serious problems at work, forced you to stop your usual activities, or resulted in you needing help from a hospital or clinic?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I have lost the trust of colleagues, missed board meetings and bills, and needed my cousin and a museum administrator to step in because I could not manage appointments, money, or public events safely on my own.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the manic symptoms caused marked impairment in social or occupational functioning, or necessitated hospitalization, which directly corresponds to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, it did get quite out of hand. I suppose I did lose the trust of my colleagues... I missed several important board meetings and just completely forgot to pay my bills. It got to the point where my cousin and one of the museum administrators had to step in. They had to take over because I just couldn't manage my appointments, or my money, or even attend public events safely by myself. 

Speaking of public events, I used to love going to the symphony. The strings section always gave me goosebumps. My cousin actually plays the cello, quite beautifully too. She has this antique cello that's been in our family for generations, supposedly made in the 1800s. It has such a rich, resonant sound. We used to go to this little tea shop after her recitals. They served the most delicate cucumber sandwiches with the crusts cut off, just like they do in England. I've always admired British etiquette, it's so refined. Did you know they have specific rules for how to stir tea? You're supposed to move the spoon back and forth from six o'clock to twelve o'clock, never in a circle. It's fascinating how many little unspoken rules there are in society. 

But yes, when I had all that energy, I really couldn't manage things on my own, and it caused quite a few problems until they stepped in to help me.

inference.note: The patient reports a duration of psychotic symptoms (hallucinations and delusions) of eight months, including at least two weeks of psychosis in the absence of mood symptoms. Additionally, she reports a history of severe manic episodes (decreased need for sleep, social/occupational dysfunction, requiring intervention). Given the prominence of the manic episodes and the persistence of psychosis outside of mood phases, Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type (F25.0) is the primary diagnostic candidate.

The presence of psychotic symptoms during both mood and non-mood states, with a documented period of at least two weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms, supports a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder, manic type.
